question: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of diarrhea and weakness after her meals for 2 weeks. She has the urge to defecate 15–20 minutes after a meal and has 3–6 bowel movements a day. She also has palpitations, sweating, and needs to lie down soon after eating. One month ago, she underwent a distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer. She had post-operative pneumonia, which was treated with cefotaxime. She returned from a vacation to Brazil 6 weeks ago. Her immunizations are up-to-date. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 51 kg (112 lb); BMI is 18.6 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a well-healed abdominal midline surgical scar. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Rectal examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "63-year-old woman with diarrhea and weakness" -> "recent distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer" -> "possible post-surgical complications" -> "hyperactive bowel sounds" -> "diarrhea after meals" -> "possible dumping syndrome" -> "dietary modifications may help" -> 85%

enhanced_information: The 63-year-old woman exhibits symptoms consistent with dumping syndrome, a common complication following distal gastrectomy, characterized by postprandial diarrhea, weakness, palpitations, and sweating. The hyperactive bowel sounds further support this diagnosis. Dietary modifications are the first-line management for dumping syndrome, focusing on smaller, more frequent meals and reducing simple carbohydrates. While stool tests (such as PCR) could be considered to rule out infectious causes, the clinical presentation strongly suggests dumping syndrome rather than an infectious etiology. Octreotide therapy may be an option if dietary modifications fail, but it is not the first step. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is dietary modifications.
